schemaNote: Extends the live 1.9.2 item schema (id/skillId/sport/difficulty/misconceptionMap) with: phase as 'P1'|'P2'|'P3' strings (live used numeric 1-3), misconceptionMap as an array of {trigger, tag, signature} objects (live used a flat trap->tag object; signatures are now explicit for audit), and new required fields archetype, standard, hintLadderRef, authoringNote, plus a full D1-convention visual object (id/type/purpose/data/annotations/reveal_beats) replacing the nullable visual/visualSpec pair. Archetype-specific bodies (parts, shownWork+questions+errorAnalysisOf, predict/reveal, interaction) are additive; scaffolded items carry per-part maps and a part-prefixed flattened item-level map so the attempt log stays reconstructable per taxonomy §3.4. v2 (QUESTION_VOICE §11 ADJUSTs): predict-reveal items may carry resolveAcceptedEquivalents, the resolve-prefixed mirror of the parts-level acceptedEquivalents field.

items.prompt: A team had 10 total runs scored after game 4 and 30 total runs after game 9. Find the team's scoring pace one move at a time.

parts.prompt: How much did the run total climb between the two snapshots (the rise)?

parts.prompt: How many games did that climb take (the run)?

misconceptionMap.signature: 4 - 9 = -5: denominator read backward relative to part (a)'s forward rise (§2.2)

parts.prompt: Now divide your rise by your run: what is the slope, in runs per game?

misconceptionMap.signature: Δy = 30 - 10 = 20 reported as the slope (§2.1; |Δx| = 5 != 1 so the trap is live)
Δx/Δy = 5/20 = 1/4 = 1/m (§2.3; |m| = 4 != 1 so the trap is live)

parts.prompt: Last one: you found a slope of 4. Which sentence says what that slope of 4 means?

choices.text: The team's run total climbs by 4 runs each game.

10 - 30 = -20 (§2.2 at the rise step)
y2 = 30 reported instead of the change (§2.8)
4 - 9 = -5 (§2.2 at the run step)
Δy = 20 as slope (§2.1)
games-per-run referent swap (§2.3 interpretation form)

visual.purpose: Support each part with the rise bracket, run bracket, and division readout appearing as the student earns them.
annotations: rise arrow --blue-on-light, run arrow --green-on-light (lesson convention, with arrowheads)

items.authoringNote: P1 on-ramp mirroring the lesson's three moves on fresh numbers (4,10)-(9,30). Traps instantiate §2.1/§2.2/§2.3/§2.6; generator constraints |Δx| != 1, |m| != 1, y1 != x1, y1 != 0 all hold and all trap values are pairwise distinct from the key 4. v2 (QUESTION_VOICE §11 ADJUST): part (d) interpretation capstone added - distractors key §2.3 (swapped referent), §2.10 (true 20-runs-over-5-games interval reading offered as the meaning of the 4), and §2.9 (proportional reading, armed by b = -6 != 0 on the line y = 4x - 6); no distractor restates the correct per-game reading (cumulative-context hazard checked).

Part (b) traps are deterministic propagations of part (a) misconceptions, so a consistent wrong model leaves a two-hit evidence trail (§3.4: 2 hits = tag active). §2.9 armed via b = 11/4 != 0; choice format sidesteps §2.9's numeric-tolerance separation concern. v2 (QUESTION_VOICE §11 ADJUSTs): meta-label 'No story.' deleted from the stem; part (d) adds the generalization capstone (compute -> use -> interpret -> generalize) as choice-for-expressions because the Phase-8 keypad is fraction-only and cannot take symbolic input; choices use exactly the lesson §6 subscript notation (x₁, y₁, x₂, y₂); distractors key §2.2 (mixed-order quotient), §2.3 (inverted quotient), §2.7 (within-point differences). Part count 4 <= 5.

The shown 2.4 equals y2/x2 = 30/12.5 exactly; the y1/x1 variant (4.4) survives as the reveal's self-contradiction, and the true slope 1.9 differs from both. items.prompt: A drive's chart passes through (2, 30) and (8, 12) - yards-to-go falling as plays go by. Build the run arrow and the rise arrow that walk from one point to the other around the right-angle corner.

interaction.manipulates: two grid-snapped directed arrows (one horizontal run, one vertical rise) placed between the plotted points and their corner

scoring.correctWhen: both arrows trace the SAME traversal: P1-to-P2 as run (2,30)->(8,30) with rise (8,30)->(8,12), or rise (2,30)->(2,12) with run (2,12)->(8,12); or P2-to-P1 as run (8,12)->(2,12) with rise (2,12)->(2,30), or rise (8,12)->(8,30) with run (8,30)->(2,30)
scoring.note: the full P2-to-P1 reversal is mathematically correct and MUST be accepted (§2.15 - point labeling is arbitrary); only mixed-direction states are wrong

misconceptionMap.trigger: run arrow points +x while rise arrow points +y (e.g. run (2,30)->(8,30) with rise (8,12)->(8,30))
misconceptionMap.signature: the two arrows walk the line in opposite directions, encoding 18/6 = +3 = -m on a visibly falling line - §2.2's arrows re-representation used as the detector

misconceptionMap.trigger: riseArrow is horizontal and runArrow is vertical (roles swapped)
misconceptionMap.signature: arrow roles encode Δx/Δy = 6/(-18) = -1/3 = 1/m (§2.3; |m| = 3 != 1)

visual.purpose: Arrow-construction canvas on a falling line, so direction consistency is a physical act rather than a notation rule.
annotations: arrowheads are mandatory - direction is the assessed object
on a mixed-direction submit, both arrows animate a walking figure that leaves the line, echoing §2.4's contradiction move
reveal_beats: Plane, both points, and the falling line appear with the empty arrow palette.
Student places and orients both arrows, then submits.
On resolve: the signed readout appears; correct reversed-traversal states get the caption 'walking the other way is fine - both arrows just have to agree.'

items.authoringNote: Direct interactive instantiation of §2.2's remediation move ('do your two arrows walk the same direction?') as a scored construct item; opposite-direction states are the deliverable's named pattern for inconsistent-subtraction-order. Accepting all four consistent traversals encodes §2.15's full-reversal-is-correct rule into the scoring contract.

items.prompt: The table shows a linear pattern: x = 0, 2, 4, 6 with y = 1, 7, 13, 19. Drag the line's two handles - one pinned at x = 0, one at x = 6 - until the line passes through every point in the table.

interaction.manipulates: the y-positions of two handles pinned at x = 0 and x = 6 (integer snap); the line through the handles renders live over the plotted table points

scoring.note: equivalent to slope (y6 - y0)/6 == 3 with intercept y0 == 1; exact match is well-defined because handles snap to integers

misconceptionMap.signature: correct slope 3 forced through the origin, dropping b = 1 - the y = (Δy/Δx)x proportionality overgeneralization (§2.9; armed because b != 0)
uses the row-to-row jump Δy = 6 as the slope while ignoring Δx = 2, building y = 6x + 1 (§2.1)

visual.purpose: Representation-transfer construction: the table is the source of truth; the student must translate its constant rate AND its start value into a line.

right_panel.live_line: solid through both handles, updating as they drag

annotations: table gap labels (+6 per 2 steps of x) are visible from first paint - reading them correctly IS the task
table points render as open dots on the plane; a point fills solid when the live line passes through it
reveal_beats: Table and plane appear; all four target dots open; handles at a neutral wrong start (y0 = 5, y6 = 11).
Student drags; dots fill as the line captures them.
On submit-correct: readout 'slope 3, starts at 1: y climbs 6 every 2 steps' appears.
On the origin-forced wrong state: the (0, 1) dot pulses - 'the pattern does not start at 0.'

items.authoringNote: Table-to-graph representation transfer (difficulty 4) with Δx = 2 between rows so the row jump (6) and the slope (3) genuinely differ - §2.1 stays live in table form. The origin-forced pattern is §2.9's stated L08-facing re-surface (drops b), caught here first. All three wrong states are exact and pairwise distinct. v2 (QUESTION_VOICE §11 ADJUST): register pass only - wording tightened; the imperative drag instruction stays (intrinsic to the archetype); one context sentence + one instruction, within the <= 2-context-sentence bound. Clean values retained: integer-snap scoring requires them.

items.prompt: A table pairs the inputs x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with the outputs y = 3, 8, 15, 24. Does y grow at one constant rate?

choices.text: Yes - a steady 7 per step, because from (1, 3) to (4, 24) it climbs 21 over 3 steps.
No - the jumps grow: +5, then +7, then +9. No single rate fits.
Yes - a steady 5 per step, because from (1, 3) to (2, 8) it climbs 5.

misconceptionMap.signature: endpoint two-point slope (24 - 3)/(4 - 1) = 7 asserted as 'the rate' of a nonconstant table - §2.14 signature (b), the required construction
first-interval rate m1 = 5 extrapolated as the rate everywhere - §2.14 signature (a) flavor; middle differences 7 and 9 betray it

visual.purpose: The middle-point betrayal: the endpoint line visibly misses the interior points, so the student's own data supplies the counterexample.
annotations: gap labels are hidden until resolve - the item assesses whether the student checks the middle unprompted
on resolve, interior points (2, 8) and (3, 15) pulse where the dashed line misses them
reveal_beats: Table alone appears (no gap labels); the student commits an answer.
On resolve: gap labels +5, +7, +9 appear down the table one at a time.
Dashed endpoint line draws on the plane and visibly misses the two middle points - 'no single line can do that.'

items.authoringNote: The required constant-vs-nonconstant discrimination item: option A is the deliverable's specified signature (endpoint two-point slope asserted as 'the rate,' §2.14(b)) on a fresh table distinct from the lesson §7 bridge table. Both traps key §2.14 through different computations (endpoints vs first interval), sharpening the boundary the lesson's 'check the middle' rule owns. v2 (QUESTION_VOICE §11 ADJUST): register pass only - the coaching clause ('look at the whole table before computing') removed so checking the middle unprompted stays the assessed behavior; interrogative close kept. Numbers untouched: the clean +5/+7/+9 first differences ARE the construct.

items.prompt: The graph shows a running back's total rushing yards. The line passes through the gridpoints (1, 50) and (5, 250). Read the axes carefully: each y-gridline is 25 yards; each x-gridline is 1 game. What is his rushing rate, in yards per game?

misconceptionMap.signature: counts gridsquares: the line rises 2 squares per 1 square right, so m*(s_x/s_y) = 50*(1/25) = 2 (§2.11; armed because s_x = 1 != s_y = 25)
Δy = 250 - 50 = 200 reported as the slope (§2.1; |Δx| = 4 != 1)

visual.purpose: Deliberately unequal axis scales so square-counting and axis-reading give different answers on the same picture (§2.11's authoring mandate).

post_resolve_overlay.axis_reading: each square up is worth 25 yards: 2 x 25 = 50 yards per game

annotations: y-axis tick labels (0, 25, 50, ... 300) all rendered - the scale is fully available
post-resolve overlay shows the counted answer and the labeled answer side by side; the axis wins
reveal_beats: Plane with unequal scales, both points, and the line appear; student answers.
On resolve: one gridsquare of rise highlights and its axis value '25 yards' labels it.
The two readings (2 squares vs 50 yards per game) appear stacked - §2.11's one-graph-two-readings counter.

items.authoringNote: Satisfies §2.11's severity note that at least one unequal-scale item must live in L06 practice, not just the gate - the error is invisible on equal-scale graphs. 50 yards per game over five games (250 total) is an authentic workhorse-back stat line. Key signature (§2.11) distinct from disc-01 (§2.14) and disc-03 (§2.9/§2.8).

items.prompt: A guard entered this season with 5 career three-pointers already made. Through 4 games this season her career total is 13; through 8 games it is 21. At what rate is she adding threes this season, per game?

choices.text: 2 per game
8 per game
3.25 per game
21 per game

misconceptionMap.signature: Δy = 21 - 13 = 8 reported as the per-game rate (§2.1; |Δx| = 4 != 1)
y1/x1 = 13/4 = 3.25 from one point (variant y2/x2 = 21/8 = 2.625 computed and excluded); armed because the 5-three head start makes b = 5 != 0 (§2.9)
y2 = 21 (the height of the graph at game 8) read as the rate (§2.8; y1 = 13 != 0, y2 != m)

visual.purpose: Foreground the head start so dividing a single snapshot is visibly wrong: the career total did not start at zero this season.

data.caption: She started the season already at 5 career threes.

annotations: the (0, 5) row renders in --text-muted with the tag 'head start' - present from first paint, because noticing it is the discrimination
on resolve: per-interval changes '+8 threes / 4 games' bracket the last two rows
reveal_beats: Full table with the head-start row appears; student answers.
On resolve: brackets show +8 over 4 games between the season snapshots, readout '8 / 4 = 2 per game.'
Caption: 'dividing 13 by 4 assumes she started at zero - she did not.'

items.authoringNote: Discriminates slope from y-value and from single-point ratio within the confusable cluster: b = 5 (career head start) arms §2.9, whose entry names this exact proportional-vs-linear boundary as the key Axis-B discriminator. Data is internally consistent (y = 2x + 5 through all three rows); 2 threes per game is authentic for a high-volume shooter. Key signature distinct from disc-01 and disc-02.
